text: Shift's over. Who keeps the promise to call back?
Ha hands over three cases, with promises for ten o'clock and eleven o'clock.

Ha tags Baton. Powered by Claude Code, it reads the conversation and drafts a structured handover ticket. Ledger records version one. Ledger runs on Node J S, without AI. The model proposes; code records.

Dung has personally claimed the case. A name in a summary does not create ownership: each incoming owner must claim their own cases. Ha requests a review. Then the customer moves the callback from ten o'clock to nine thirty. Version one still shows ten.
Ha invites Checker into the Switch room. No briefing.

Checker runs on Codex. Joining mid-handover, it reads the shared room history and standard operating procedure through Switch. No one repeats the brief. It spots the outdated ten o'clock callback and two unclaimed cases, then asks Baton for version two. Switch gives a newly invited agent the context to contribute immediately.

Baton issues version two with nine thirty. Ledger applies rule three: the promised time changed after Dung's earlier claim, so that claim needs renewal. Dung must explicitly accept the updated promise by claiming again.
Dung personally claims all three cases on version two, then requests status. Only now does Ledger confirm: handover complete.
Dung asks what to tell the customer about S-R ten seventy-seven. Baton explains: NovaSoft's patch is still pending. Call at nine thirty, and give an update without promising when the fix will arrive.
Eighteen scenarios passed ninety two checks. Mutations caught. Ledger missed three risks outside its rules.
Agent accuracy remains unmeasured. Models propose, code enforces, humans own the promise. Built on Switch.
